patch.value: Intent-scoped read projections: a command returns exactly the fields the declared intent consumes, so agents stop paying for fields they discard

pm get returns a full item projection whether the caller is about to close the item, review its evidence, implement it, or merely confirm it exists. The agent then discards most of it. The same is true of list and context: the projection is a property of the command, not of the purpose. Intent is the missing dimension and it is cheap to declare — an agent always knows why it is reading. Introduce a contract-declared intent on read surfaces (for example orient, implement, review, close, triage, link) where each intent names exactly the field set it consumes, and the command returns that set. Intents are contract data, discoverable through the contracts surface and extensible per workspace, so a domain built on the SDK declares its own intents rather than inheriting a project-management vocabulary. This composes with, and does not duplicate, the token-budget work: the budget decides how much output is allowed, the intent decides which fields are worth spending it on, and the relevance engine decides which items are worth including. Field selection stays honest: an intent that omits a field an agent then needs must be discoverable as a miss, so intent definitions can be corrected by evidence.

Read surfaces accept a declared intent, and each intent names its exact field set in contract data rather than in code; Omitting the intent preserves today's default projection byte-for-byte, proven by a snapshot test; Intents are discoverable through the contracts surface and extensible by workspace configuration and packages, so a non-project-management domain can declare its own; A measured token delta per intent versus the default projection is published as evidence, per command and per result size; Requesting an intent that a workspace has not declared fails with the one canonical unknown-value error and a nearest-match suggestion; Intent selection composes with the token budget and the relevance engine without any of the three overriding the others, proven by a test that exercises all three together
The field set of a read is decided by the reader's purpose rather than by the command name
Field-level waste is paid on every read of every item; at a million items and thousands of agents it is one of the largest recurring token costs in the system
Adds one declared dimension to read surfaces; existing default projections stay unchanged so no caller is broken
Common agent loops read materially fewer tokens per item without losing any field they actually use

value.text:
Intent-split evidence measured 2026-07-25 on `pm next --json` (2,022-item workspace, default flags). Payload breakdown by top-level key, in bytes:

- blocked: 5,450 (47% of the response)
- decision_needed: 2,163 (19%)
- ready: 2,116 (18%)
- recommended: 660 (6%)
- filters 214, summary 133, truncation 27

The agent asked one question — what should I work on next — and 66% of the answer describes work it explicitly cannot start. The recommendation itself, the actual answer, is 6%. This is the clearest single case for intent-scoped projection in the CLI: `next` today serves three distinct intents (pick my next task; show me what is stuck; show me what needs a human decision) in one unconditional payload, and an agent pays for all three every time.

Note also that `--fields` is available on list (5 references in help), search (4), and get (3), but absent from `next` entirely and nearly absent from `context` (1). The two commands an agent runs first, and most often, are the two with the least projection control.

Suggested intent names when this item defines the vocabulary, so the split follows the existing envelope rather than inventing new shapes: `--for next` (recommended only), `--for triage` (blocked + blockers), `--for decisions` (decision_needed). Companion buckets stay reachable, never removed — the pm-0z7n alias-preservation rule applies to output shape, not just spellings.

value.text: Cost of the mandated orientation sequence, measured 2026-07-28 on the live 2,172-item tracker. The four commands AGENTS.md requires before creating work cost 16,631 bytes in default TOON output: context --limit 10 is 7,517, search with a ten-row limit 3,980, list-open --limit 20 4,759, list-in-progress --limit 20 375. Adding next --limit 5 at 8,901 brings the preamble an agent pays before touching any work to 25,532 bytes, about 6,400 tokens. next is the single largest contributor at 35 percent of the total, consistent with the earlier finding that it spends 47 percent of its own payload on the blocked companion. Encoding delta measured on the same call: context --limit 10 --json is 10,277 bytes against 7,517 for TOON, 37 percent more. This is the number that justifies this item existing: an intent projection that answers what should I do next about X in one call is competing against a 25 kB four-call preamble, not against a single cheap read. Cross-referenced on pm-5t33or as an output-cost datapoint and on pm-n7rr as a simplification lever.

value.author: harness:claude-code
value.text:
Orientation cost re-measured at build 2026.7.29 on the real 2,193-item tracker.

The four commands the repository's own agent guidance mandates before creating work now total 17,840 bytes, about 4,460 tokens: context --limit 10 at 8,178 B, search with a keyword --limit 10 at 4,089 B, list-open --limit 20 at 5,086 B, list-in-progress --limit 20 at 487 B. The same preamble measured 25,532 bytes, about 6,383 tokens, on 2026-07-28. That is a 30 percent reduction in one day, attributable to the lean mutation envelopes and omission receipts that landed in the 2026-07-29 lanes rather than to any change in this item's scope.

Adjacent per-command costs measured in the same run, for the intent-projection design: next --limit 5 8,651 B, get pm-doxj --depth brief 4,027 B, stats 440 B, validate --json 108,652 B, validate plain 22,479 B.

Two points this sharpens for the --for projection design. First, the preamble is now dominated by context and next, which overlap heavily in content - both assemble an active working set, and an agent that runs both pays twice for one answer. Second, stats at 440 bytes proves an orientation answer can be delivered in three figures of bytes; the gap between 440 and 4,460 is the space a declared intent should be able to close.
